extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and educated readers interested in epic poetry and Miltonic style
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing and judging epic or heroic poetry (as illustrated by praise of Milton's Paradise Lost): invocation, similes, characterisation, wondrous incidents, learned catalogues, and pacing. Focuses on high poetic diction and classical models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain, simple, unadorned opening lines / Invocation
rubrics_metrics.description: The opening lines (invocation) should be plain, simple and unadorned, conforming to the example of Homer and the precept of Horace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton's lines 'Of Man's first disobedience...' are cited as 'perhaps as plain, simple and unadorned as any of the whole Poem.' Invocation should address the proper source of inspiration for the subject (e.g., the Muse that inspired Moses / the Holy Spirit when dealing with creation) and lead naturally into the fable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate Muse / invocation suited to subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Invoke the Muse or inspirer that best fits the poem's subject (e.g., the Muse who inspired Moses or the Holy Spirit for a poem about Creation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper praises Milton's invocation to the Muse who inspired Moses and the Holy Spirit as 'very properly made' for a work turning on the Creation of the World; the choice of inspirer should reflect the poem's sources and theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural, happy transition to the fable
rubrics_metrics.description: The transition from invocation/exordium into the fable should be felicitous and natural, rising into noble language and sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton's exordium is praised: 'This whole Exordium rises very happily into noble Language and Sentiment, as I think the Transition to the Fable is exquisitely beautiful and natural.' Strive for a smooth movement from praise/invocation into story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce grand circumstances to evoke awe (use of marvelous/noble incidents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include high, astonishing circumstances (e.g., angels entranced for nine days after the Fall) that are nobly imagined and awaken the reader's wonder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The Nine Days Astonishment, in which the Angels lay entranced...' is called 'a noble Circumstance, and very finely imagined.' Use such elevated incidents to produce sublime effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive and coherent world-building (mythic geography and laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: Create striking, coherent features of the poem's cosmos (e.g., division of Hell into seas of fire and firm ground; exclusion of Hope) that demonstrate fertile invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise is given to 'The Division of Hell into Seas of Fire, and into firm Ground...with that particular Circumstance of the Exclusion of Hope' as instances of great invention. Such features should be imaginative yet internally consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex, multifaceted characterisation of major antagonists (show passions interwoven)
rubrics_metrics.description: Depict principal antagonists by artfully interweaving their principal passions (pride, envy, revenge, obstinacy, despair, impenitence) so their speeches and behavior reveal a consistent, composite character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton's Satan is praised: 'His Pride, Envy and Revenge, Obstinacy, Despair and Impenitence, are all of them very artfully interwoven.' The first speech should be a 'complication' of these passions and set up subsequent appearances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match sentiments to character and nature
rubrics_metrics.description: A character's sentiments and speeches must be suitable to their established nature (e.g., Satan's sentiments are 'answerable to his Character' and fitting for an exalted but depraved created being).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure consistency between statement and character: 'His Sentiments are every way answerable to his Character, and suitable to a created Being of the most exalted and most depraved Nature.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle theological or impious material with artistic safety
rubrics_metrics.description: When a poem contains impious or theologically charged utterances by characters, present them as absurd or without real substance so as not to shock a religious reader; allow antagonist to occasionally confess truths (e.g., Omnipotence) to sustain credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper notes Milton 'has taken care to introduce none that is not big with absurdity, and incapable of shocking a Religious Reader' and that Satan 'frequently confesses his Omnipotence.' Present theological transgression as rhetorically effective rather than blasphemous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pathos and emotional complexity (tears, remorse) to deepen character
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce moments of genuine pathos (e.g., Satan bursting into tears over those he ruined) to add emotional depth and complexity to characters, even villains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example passage: 'Thrice he assayed... Tears such as Angels weep, burst forth.' Such moments enhance the reader's imagination and the moral/psychological dimension of the poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ learned catalogues and classical parallels to enrich the poem
rubrics_metrics.description: Use catalogues (e.g., of evil spirits) with learned allusions and descriptions of places of worship, drawing on classical models like Homer's Catalogue of Ships or Virgil's lists to prepare the mind for characters' speeches and behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'Catalogue of Evil Spirits' is praised for 'abundance of Learning' and for preparing the reader; classical precedent strengthens epic authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide explanatory groundwork for marvelous events to retain plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: When introducing marvellous or supernatural occurrences, supply earlier explanatory passages or plausible mechanics (e.g., spirits contracting/enlarging shapes) so later marvels feel probable rather than arbitrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton's explanation that spirits can 'transform themselves by Contractions or Enlargement of their Dimensions' makes later marvels 'probable'—the French critics called such a passage 'Marvellous, but at the same time probable.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve hierarchical distinctions within supernatural rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when allowing supernatural transformations, maintain hierarchical or rank-based exceptions (e.g., lower spirits may contract but first-rank spirits preserve natural dimensions) to add refinement and nobility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton refines the thought: 'notwithstanding the vulgar...contracted their Forms, those of the first Rank and Dignity still preserved their natural Dimensions.' Such nuances elevate conception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid set-pieces: architecture, light, and sensory spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Stage grand set-pieces (e.g., Pandæmonium) with vivid sensory description—architecture rising 'like an Exhalation', starry lamps, artificial illuminations—to create awe and poetic splendor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passages cited: 'Anon out of the Earth a Fabrick huge Rose like an Exhalation...' and the 'arched Roof... many a Row Of Starry Lamps'—use striking, concrete imagery and simile to animate vast scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop similes into extended, illuminating episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: When using similes, do not stop at a short point of likeness; run the simile on until it grows into a 'glorious Image or Sentiment' often foreign to the occasion, thereby producing a sublime entertainment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay observes Milton 'never quits his Simile till it rises to some very great Idea' and compares similes to short episodes; allow a simile to unfold into a larger imaginative scene rather than a terse decorative phrase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comparisons to amuse, relieve, and instruct (pace the reader)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce comparisons not only to illustrate but to amuse and relax the reader—frequently disengaging them from too painful attention to the main subject and leading them into agreeable images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing Boileau: 'Comparisons... are not introduced only to illustrate and embellish the Discourse, but to amuse and relax the Mind of the Reader.' Use comparisons for variety and pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow general resemblance in comparisons; avoid excessive nicety
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparisons need not correspond exactly in every point; a general resemblance suffices—overly exact comparison favors mere rhetoric and epigram rather than true poetic imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'It is not necessary in Poetry for the Points of the Comparison to correspond with one another exactly... too much Nicety in this Particular favours of the Rhetorician and Epigrammatist.' Prefer broad, fruitful likenesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ noble similes and allusions modeled on Homer and Virgil
rubrics_metrics.description: Use noble similes and classical allusions that expand into great ideas rather than small witty turns; such similes should produce variety and lofty entertainment suitable to an heroic poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay praises Milton for similes 'of the Sun in an Eclipse, of the Sleeping Leviathan, of the Bees swarming about their Hive' and recommends following Homer/Virgil in making similes long enough to yield impressive images.
